raw_text:
Transcaval access is a deliberately created, temporary cavo-aortic tract that permits large-bore retrograde aortic access from the femoral vein. The concept emerged from preclinical work showing that a guidewire energized with electrosurgery could cross from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the adjacent abdominal aorta, that large sheaths could be delivered, and that the tract could be closed without catastrophic retroperitoneal hemorrhage because aortic bleeding preferentially decompresses into the low-pressure venous lumen rather than freely into the retroperitoneum [1]. Initial human experience in otherwise ineligible transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) candidates demonstrated feasibility and established the essential procedural sequence: computed-tomography (CT) target selection, caval-to-aortic electrosurgical crossing into a prepositioned snare, large-bore sheath delivery from the femoral vein, valve implantation, and closure with an occluder device [2].

Planning is the determinant of safety. Multidetector CT is used to identify a calcium-free aortic window, adequate distance from renal arteries, iliac bifurcation and lumbar branches, absence of interposed bowel or other vulnerable structures, and a fluoroscopic projection that makes the aorta and IVC coaxial at the target [3]. Procedural tutorials and contemporary best-practice documents emphasize meticulous equipment preparation, arterial bailout access, availability of covered stents and occlusion balloons, anticoagulation reversal before closure, and use of a “buddy” wire to maintain access during device deployment [4,8]. Special scenarios—including crossing a prosthetic aortic graft—have been reported, but should be reserved for centers with advanced CT-planning and bailout capability [5].

The most robust clinical evidence remains in TAVR. In the prospective NHLBI transcaval TAVR study, access was successful in 99 of 100 attempted patients and device success was high, although early bleeding and vascular events reflected the prohibitive-risk population and the off-label use of permeable nitinol closure devices [6]. One-year imaging follow-up was reassuring: no late major vascular complications were attributed to the transcaval tract, most fistulas closed spontaneously, and persistent fistula patency was not clearly associated with heart-failure admission or mortality [7]. Subsequent reports and pooled analyses have suggested high procedural success and improving complication rates over time, likely reflecting operator learning, smaller TAVR delivery systems, better CT selection, and refined closure technique [10-13].

Compared with other alternative access routes, transcaval offers distinctive advantages. It is fully percutaneous, avoids thoracotomy and apical myocardial injury, preserves upper-extremity and carotid arteries, and permits the operator to work from a familiar femoral position. Observational comparisons suggest outcomes comparable with transcarotid, transaxillary/subclavian and other nonfemoral approaches in selected patients, although randomized data are lacking and confounding by anatomy, frailty and center expertise remains substantial [14-21]. Registry analyses have generally favored peripheral over transthoracic alternative access, supporting the broader migration away from transapical and direct-aortic routes [16,21]. Because neurologic risk, vascular calcification, dialysis access, prior bypass grafts, severe lung disease and hostile chest anatomy influence the relative attractiveness of each route, transcaval should be considered one option in a multidisciplinary access algorithm rather than a universal default [18-21].

Adverse events cluster around crossing, sheath delivery and closure. Potential complications include retroperitoneal bleeding, aortic dissection, persistent aortocaval fistula, pseudoaneurysm, device embolization, need for covered stent placement, transfusion and acute kidney injury. Standardized endpoint definitions from VARC-2 and VARC-3 are essential when comparing series, because bleeding and vascular complications may otherwise be inconsistently classified [22,23]. Importantly, transcaval access depends on aortic wall compliance and an adequate noncalcified target; circumferential calcium, severe leftward aortic displacement, interposed structures, very short landing zones, and inability to place bailout equipment are relative or absolute contraindications [8].

Although developed for structural heart intervention, the transcaval principle has also been extended to emergency large-bore mechanical circulatory support, where femoral arterial obstruction or limb ischemia may preclude Impella-class devices [9]. Experience in endovascular aortic repair and systematic reviews of transcaval endovascular interventions reinforce the broader large-bore-access concept, but structural heart practice remains dominated by TAVR [10]. As TAVR has expanded from inoperable and high-risk patients to intermediate- and low-risk populations, transfemoral access has become safer and smaller-profile, narrowing the population needing alternative access [24-29]. Nevertheless, contemporary registry data show that a meaningful minority of patients still require nonfemoral strategies [30]. Future progress will depend on dedicated crossing and closure systems, prospective comparative studies against transcarotid and transaxillary access, training standards, and careful reporting of late fistula, bleeding and vascular outcomes.
